taxonomy.subtopic: Diastolic left atrial-left ventricular gradient and pulmonary venous hypertension

questions.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman who emigrated from a region with limited access to antibiotics has progressive exertional dyspnea and occasional palpitations. Auscultation reveals a loud S1, an opening snap, and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Echocardiography shows thickened commissurally fused mitral leaflets and marked left atrial enlargement.

Which hemodynamic abnormality is most directly responsible for her pulmonary symptoms?

options.text_html: A systolic pressure gradient from the left ventricle to the aorta
A persistent diastolic pressure gradient from the left atrium to the left ventricle
Regurgitant flow from the left ventricle to the left atrium during systole
Reduced right atrial pressure caused by impaired venous return
Premature closure of the pulmonic valve during inspiration

questions.explanation_html: Obstruction at the mitral valve prevents normal diastolic emptying of the left atrium. Elevated left atrial pressure is transmitted backward to pulmonary veins and capillaries, causing dyspnea and edema. The defining hemodynamic lesion is a diastolic gradient across the stenotic mitral valve, with elevated upstream left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: This describes aortic stenosis and does not explain an opening snap or apical diastolic rumble.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Mitral regurgitation produces a holosystolic murmur rather than a diastolic rumble with an opening snap.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Mitral stenosis raises pulmonary venous and eventually right-sided pressures rather than lowering right atrial pressure.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Pulmonic valve timing is not the primary cause of pulmonary venous congestion in mitral stenosis.

questions.educational_objective: Connect rheumatic mitral stenosis to a diastolic transmitral gradient, left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation risk, and pulmonary venous hypertension.
